speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The allegations seem to concern, primarily, three matters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I, therefore, have no choice but to address them promptly and publicly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I also have to do so in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Under the Constitution, the Prime Minister is a person who commands the confidence of the majority of the Members of Parliament (MPs).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As their PM, I have a duty to explain myself to MPs and to rebut in Parliament the allegations against me and my Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I know many Singaporeans are upset by this issue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are tired of the subject and wish it would end.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I, too, am upset that things have reached this state.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a son, I am pained at the anguish this strife would have caused my parents to feel if they were still alive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I intend to clear the air today to explain the matter fully and to answer all questions on the matter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am not here to make a case against my siblings.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What is private, I will try to resolve privately.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But what is public, I have to explain and render account.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To respond to these allegations of abuse of power, I will have to go into some background about 38 Oxley Road and the family discussions on the house so that Members can make sense of the allegations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But my account will inevitably be from my perspective.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, I will try my best to be objective and factual.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I will cover the discussions on 38 Oxley Road when Mr Lee Kuan Yew was alive, what happened after Mr Lee passed away, and then, where the matter stands today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After my mother died in 2010, my father wrote to Cabinet to put his position on the record.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This the first note you have in the bundle which is dated 27 October 2010.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is a letter from Mr Lee to the Cabinet and it reads: "I have discussed this with my family many a time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They agreed with me that 38 Oxley Road should not be kept as a kind of relic for people to tramp through.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Take photos of it or whatever else they want, but demolish it after I am gone.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have seen too many places which are kept frozen in time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My most vivid memory is that of Nehru's final home, that of the British Naval Commander of the Indian Ocean Fleet in New Delhi." Actually, it was another British General's home but you get the point. "It was once a grand building.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Kept as a monument with people tramping in and out, it became shabby.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: A few months later, in January 2011, my father published the book, "Hard Truths to Keep Singapore Going".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In the book, the question of preserving his house came up.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He said, "I have told the Cabinet, when I am dead, demolish it".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He explained again that he did not want the house to become a shambles.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The cost of preservation would be high because the house was built over a hundred years ago and had no foundation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If the house was demolished and planning rules could change, the value of the land, as well as the surrounding plots, would go up.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: However, after "Hard Truths" was published, there was a strong public pushback.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Many Singaporeans did not agree with Mr Lee.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This was, after all, the house of Singapore's founding Prime Minister, where important political decisions were made that shaped the future of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We are a young nation and what the house represents is of particular significance to our history and nationhood.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, in March 2011, my father asked some newspaper editors for their views.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: All the editors replied that they would like it to be kept, given its historical importance and heritage value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Guntor Sadali, then editor of Berita Harian, wrote to my father: "I was personally shocked and sad, when I first read about you saying that you wanted the house demolished after you are gone.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The historical value of the house is priceless…if we demolish it, our next generations will regret it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We should avoid making this mistake." Mr Lim Jim Koon, then editor of Lianhe Zaobao, suggested that the house be conserved and turned into a museum, like the Sun Yat Sen Memorial Hall.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: These were not the answers my father hoped to get.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My father then wanted to leave the decision to his children.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But we told him that only he could decide.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He then said his decision was to knock it down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I told him that in that case he should tell the editors and put it on record.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After the General Election in May 2011, Mr Lee retired from the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He then decided to put his views on record again.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And that is the second letter in the bundle you have, 20 July 2011.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He wrote to Cabinet to reiterate that he wanted the house knocked down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It says: "I have previously written to Cabinet that the house should be demolished.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It has no foundations and it is in poor condition.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is difficult to maintain if people start tramping through the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Whenever there is piling in Cluny Road for new homes, hairline cracks begin to appear on the walls.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, keeping the house is too hazardous and costly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I, therefore, repeat my wish to have the house demolished when I am no longer alive." This is the letter which I referred to when I addressed Parliament on 13 April 2015 and said he expressed his wish that the house be knocked down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, he wrote this on 20 July 2011.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When I saw this letter the next morning, that means, 21 July 2011, I immediately invited Mr Lee to make his case in person to Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After the meeting, my father continued to ponder over how to deal with the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, even before the Cabinet meeting, he had been discussing with the family how to go about demolishing the house and redeveloping the site.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We explored in the family all kinds of permutations − to demolish the house and redevelop the site, maximise value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We discussed who to inherit the property, whether it should be one of the children or several of the children, whether to demolish the house before or after my father died, whether to donate the proceeds to charity after the site was redeveloped and, if so, which children would share in the donation, and which charities to donate to.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He even had some ideas which charities he wanted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Ho Ching and I knew my father's wishes and also my mother's feelings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We also knew how Cabinet and the public viewed the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We started discussing alternatives with my father to see how best we could fulfil his wishes in the event that the house could not be demolished.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My father's concern was that the house should not become run-down and dilapidated and that it should not be an expensive burden to maintain.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My late mother had a different concern: privacy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: She felt strongly that her private living spaces should always remain private.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: She had been most distressed at the thought of people tramping through her personal spaces, after she and my father had passed away, to gawk at how they had lived.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Even when not so familiar people came into the house for one reason or the other to meet her or my father, she would complain afterwards, "You could see them looking around, eyes opened, to try and find out how we live." She resented it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, Ho Ching and I came up with a proposal to renovate the house to change the inside completely.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Demolish the private living spaces to preserve the privacy of the family, keep the basement dining room, which was of historical significance, strengthen the structure which was decaying and create a new and separate living area, so the house could be lived in.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: By redevelopment, he meant remove the private spaces and renovate the house but without knocking it down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And you have the letter with you: "Cabinet members were unanimous that 38 Oxley Road should not be demolished as I wanted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have reflected on this and decided that if 38 Oxley Road is to be preserved, it needs to have its foundations reinforced and the whole building refurbished.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It must then be let out for people to live in.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: An empty building will soon decline and decay." Ho Ching and I, therefore, proceeded along these lines.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We kept the family fully informed of our considerations and our intentions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We emailed everyone, including my father, my sister, my brother and his wife.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: No one raised any objections to the plan.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My father met the architect, went through the proposal, and approved the scheme to reinforce the foundations and renovate the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have just given Members the first page of the Grant of Written Permission.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But the first page puts the key points − name and address of developer: Lee Kuan Yew, 38 Oxley Road; date of application received and so on; particulars of decision: planning permission is granted under section 14(4) of the Planning Act for the application referred to, details are set out in Part 3, subject to conditions in Part 4, additional notes in Part 5.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As far as I knew, that was how the family had settled the matter, rationally, amicably while Mr Lee was still alive which is what he had hoped to achieve and strived very hard to achieve.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I heard nothing to the contrary until after my father died.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I would ask each of my children to ensure our wishes with respect to the demolition of the house be carried out.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If our children are unable to demolish the house as a result of any changes in the laws, rules or regulations binding them, it is my wish that the house never be opened to others except my children, their families and descendants.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My view on this has been made public before and remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My statement of wishes in this paragraph 7 may be publicly disclosed notwithstanding that the rest of my will is private." This whole thing is one paragraph 7 but I have broken it up so you can see the different sections.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The following day, I had to speak in Parliament on how we would honour Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The question of 38 Oxley Road was bound to come up.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There were already suggestions from the public on what to do with the house, including turning it into a museum and memorial.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I was personally in a difficult position because I was both Mr Lee's son and the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, at the reading of the will, I discussed with my siblings what I could say about the house in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Hsien Yang for the first time objected to the renovation plans that my father had approved.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He wanted the house to be knocked down immediately.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I pointed out that his position now was different from what the family had discussed and agreed upon.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But it was not possible to knock down the house immediately, anyway, because my sister, Wei Ling then said she intended to continue to stay in the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We also discussed what I should say in Parliament regarding my father's wishes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I wanted to read out Mr Lee's 27 December 2011 letter to the Cabinet, stating his view on what to do with the house if it is to be preserved.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I also wanted to read out the demolition clause in his will, in full.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I decided that I had to do so, and I said so.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So that my father's views would be on the record and Singaporeans could know accurately what his thinking had been.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Later that evening, I discovered that my siblings had issued a statement which contained the full demolition clause.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In Parliament the next day, I made a statement which I had cleared with my key Cabinet colleagues because I was speaking as Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I read out both the letter to Cabinet and the whole demolition clause.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I said "we should not rush into making decisions on this matter, especially so soon after Mr Lee has passed away.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We should allow some time to pass, consider the ideas carefully, and make calm, considered decisions which will stand the test of time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We want to honour Mr Lee, but we must do so in the right way." I stated that my father's position on 38 Oxley Road had been unwavering all these years, that he wanted the house knocked down, and that, as a son, I wanted to see my father's wishes carried out.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I told Parliament that since my sister was going to continue living in 38 Oxley Road, there was no immediate issue of demolition and no need for the Government to make any decision now.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As and when my sister was no longer living there, the government of the day would consider the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After the Parliament Sitting, I took two major steps.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This was formally recorded in the Cabinet minutes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: From that point on, I have been out of the loop whenever the Government handles matters concerning the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I play no part in any of the discussions or decisions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Whenever Cabinet deliberates on the house, for example, when it set up a Ministerial Committee, I absent myself, and Deputy Prime Minister Teo chairs the meeting.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My second major action, after my father died, was to divest myself of the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Soon after the Parliament Sitting, I learned that my siblings were unhappy that I was getting the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Subsequently, I made a fresh proposal to sell the house to my brother at fair market value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This time we reached agreement, this was December 2015.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And we also agreed that my brother and I would each donate half the value of the house to charity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We both did so, and in addition I topped up another half myself.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In other words, I myself gave away the full value of the house that I had inherited.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And, together, my brother and I have donated one-and-a-half times the value of the house to charity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, if you understand that properly, the house comes to me, I sell it to my brother for the market value, he gives me the value of the house, so many dollars, I give half of those dollars to charity, he gets the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In addition, he gives the same amount, half the value of the house to charity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On top of that, I separately give half the value of the house to charity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have given Members the background to 38 Oxley Road, our discussions when my father was alive and what happened after my father passed away.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There is, in substance, no longer anything for my siblings and me to dispute over on the matter of the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I really am not sure, but one possible factor may be a difference in views between me and my siblings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The difference is over this question: what did my father think about the house, apart from demolition?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Was his view black and white, all or nothing − demolish the house no matter what?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Or was he prepared to consider alternatives should demolition not be possible?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings' view is that my father absolutely wanted to demolish the house, with no compromise.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And they point to the first half of the demolition clause as evidence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is the first section that Members have in the handout.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And they say that if he considered any alternatives, such as the next section of the handout, that it was only because he was under duress.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because the Government had the power to prevent him or his heirs from knocking it down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My view is that while my father wanted the house to be demolished, he was prepared to consider alternatives should the Government decide otherwise.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Indeed, he put it in writing and approved alternative architectural plans which were submitted to URA, as I explained earlier, and approved by URA.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Next, we have to look at the full demolition clause, and not just the first half, and the full clause shows that my father did accept alternatives.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Further, I have pointed out some unusual circumstances surrounding how the last will was prepared, which are relevant because of the weight that my siblings put on the demolition clause in the last will.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Despite this difference in views, I still see no need for argument.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have submitted my views to the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I will leave it in the good hands of the Committee.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There is, therefore, no reason at all for anybody to feel "pushed into a corner" by the Committee, as my brother has claimed to be.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Regrettably, my siblings have now gone public and accused me of abusing my office.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There are very few specifics in their charges.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But because their father is Mr Lee Kuan Yew, their accusations gain some credibility and I have to take their charges seriously, which is why I am here addressing them in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings have given scant details of the charge, but my brother has cited as a "prime example" the setting up of the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have already explained that I have recused myself.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo is in charge of this matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I had nothing to do with the decision to set up the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not give any instructions to the Ministerial Committee or its members.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My only dealing with the Committee has been to respond to their requests in writing by formal correspondence, no different from my siblings' dealings with the Committee.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This is the right and proper way to handle a conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings argue that even though I have recused myself, the Ministers are my subordinates and, therefore, the Ministerial Committee cannot be independent from me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, they say this of Parliament itself.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And this cannot be right because if the Ministers are subordinates and cannot be independent, the Ministerial Committee cannot be independent.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Then the Cabinet minus me cannot be independent.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What is the process for dealing with the matter concerning the Prime Minister's personal matters?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But the process which we have embarked on, me recusing myself on the Cabinet, minus me dealing with the matter, is the standard practice for a person facing a potential conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He takes himself out from handling the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He does not participate in making any decisions about it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I myself do not deal with the matter at all.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I take no part in discussions or decisions concerning the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Ministers and officials report to and take directions from Deputy Prime Minister Teo on all 38 Oxley Road matters.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Suppose instead that I had decided as Prime Minister to knock the down the house and had pushed that decision through without allowing the Government to consider the alternatives, weigh the considerations and go through due process, just because it was what my father wanted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That would have been a real abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That would have gone against the whole system of rules and values that Mr Lee Kuan Yew spent his whole life upholding and building up.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The second issue my siblings accused me of is separate from the house itself.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My siblings have accused me of improperly obtaining this Deed which was between them and NHB.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They say I obtained the Deed as Prime Minister, and gave it to my lawyers, and that was wrong.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Deed was signed by my sister and brother, who were acting for my father's estate.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I was one of the beneficiaries of the estate.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I was entitled to be consulted by my siblings before they did this, but I was not consulted.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In June 2015, Minister Lawrence Wong updated me on a major SG50 exhibition on our founding fathers.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He told me the exhibition included artefacts from Oxley Road and described the conditions attached to the gift.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He subsequently gave me the Deed, which I had not seen it before.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As Prime Minister, I had every right to see it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The terms were onerous and unreasonable to NHB.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For example, whenever NHB displayed the items, it also had to display them with the first half of the demolition clause.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But only the first half, which said that Mr Lee wanted the house knocked down, and not the second half of the clause which stated what Mr Lee wanted done if the house could not be knocked down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This partial selective disclosure would mislead the public on Mr Lee's intentions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, this was not a gift at all.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr and Mrs Lee Kuan Yew had gifted many items to NHB during their lives, and they had never imposed any conditions on their gifts remotely like these.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What Lee Wei Ling and Lee Hsien Yang had imposed on NHB was wrong.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Discovering all this, as Prime Minister, I had to act.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Otherwise, people might later wrongly think that I was party to this.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is nonsensical to say that because I saw the Deed in my official capacity, I could not raise the matter with a family member.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If I come across anyone doing something wrong, even family, maybe especially family, it is my duty to put a stop to it and set them right if I can.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In the same way, if any Minister discovers, in the course of his official work, that a family member is dealing improperly with some Government agency or seeking to take advantage of the Government, truly the Minister must take this up with the family member and get him or her to stop.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is what the code of conduct is for.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This is expected of anyone in a public position, especially me, as Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I, therefore, wrote to my siblings through lawyers to object to what they had done.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On the Government's side, I told Minister Lawrence Wong to take instructions from Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean on this matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I believe this was the correct and proper way for me to handle the Deed of Gift.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Third, my siblings have made allegations about nepotism, concerning my wife and my son, Hongyi.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And that I want 38 Oxley Road kept standing, in order to inherit my father's credibility and bolster my standing.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Hongyi, my son, has publicly said he is not interested in politics.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Nor have I pushed him to enter politics.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My wife, Ho Ching, is the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Temasek Holdings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As CEO, she reports to the Board, chaired by Mr Lim Boon Heng.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As a company, Temasek Holdings answers to its shareholder, the Ministry of Finance, under Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have every confidence that both Mr Lim Boon Heng and Minister Heng Swee Keat understand the meaning of good corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is the Temasek Board which appoints the CEO, and the appointment has to be confirmed by the President, who is advised by the Council of Presidential Advisors (CPA).

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If Ho Ching ever behaves improperly, I have no doubt that the Temasek Board, the President and CPA know what their duty is.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Regarding the house and how its continued existence enhances my aura as Prime Minister, if I needed such magic properties to bolster my standing after 13 years as your Prime Minister, I must be in a pretty sad state.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if Singaporeans believe that such magic works in Singapore, I think Singapore would be in an even sadder state.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Now, Mdm Speaker, may I have your permission to say some words in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, it is with a heavy heart that I speak before you today in Parliament, to explain my position to Members of Parliament and Singaporeans on this matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Over the past few weeks, the dispute between me and my siblings has become public, creating anxiety amongst many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That my family is in discord is sad.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What is even sadder is to see the legacy Mr Lee Kuan Yew painstakingly built throughout his life besmirched overnight.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Everyone hopes that this matter can be resolved and we end this altercation quickly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I would also like to see this matter resolved quickly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: However, the joint release my siblings made do not pertain to just family matters.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am, therefore, compelled to refute these baseless allegations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have explained the details in my English speech.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After my father passed away, as the eldest son in the family, I naturally wanted to carry out my father's wishes and I did my best to settle the differences between me and my siblings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But as the Prime Minister, I must also take into account the country's interest and allow the Government to deal with matters relating to Mr Lee's house in an impartial manner.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am caught between these two conflicting roles, so I have done my best to keep my private interest and my public duties separate.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Barely a month after my father's passing, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean was put in charge of this matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am not involved and do not interfere.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Whenever the Cabinet deliberates on the house, for example, when it set up a Ministerial Committee, I absent myself and do not participate in the discussions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As the eldest son in the family, it is my duty to protect my parents' and family's reputation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My father willed 38 Oxley Road to me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Later, I discovered that my siblings were not pleased about this.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I did not want any monetary benefit from the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I thought that having sold the house, my siblings would be satisfied as I no longer have any interest in the house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I did not expect that they would disregard the family's reputation and air this matter in public, by making baseless allegations against me and the Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As the elder brother, I really do not know what else I should or can do.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Parliament is a solemn platform where MPs are free to question and criticise the Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew was in a similar situation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Many years ago, my father and I purchased some private property which drew criticism and affected the Government's reputation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong was then Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He asked us to clarify the issue in Parliament and be subject to questioning by the MPs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: After that Parliamentary session, we cleared all the doubts that Singaporeans had and restored their trust and confidence in the Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I will open myself to questioning by MPs, including opposition MPs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I want to explain this matter clearly and eliminate all doubts.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The family matter is an emotional one, and it is not likely that it can be resolved fully.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But, still, I hope that someday there will be a reconciliation among the siblings.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In the meantime, the nation must come first.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I must maintain the people's trust in the Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I must assure them this remains an incorruptible, effective and impartial Government, all key to Singapore's survival.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Once again, I regret the confusion and trouble my family matter has caused.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I hope this Parliamentary session will clear the air.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My team and I will continue to do our utmost to serve the people.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, may I now continue in English?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have brought this matter to Parliament because Singaporeans are entitled to a full answer from me and my Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Parliament may not be a Court of law, but it is the highest body in the land.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is also where my Government and I are accountable to MPs and to the people of Singapore Many people have asked me why I am not taking legal action, to challenge the will, sue for defamation or take some other legal action to put a stop to this and clear my name.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In normal circumstances, in fact, in any other imaginable circumstance than this, I would have sued immediately, because the accusation of the abuse of power is a very grave one, however baseless it may be.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And it is, in fact, an attack not just on me, but on the integrity of the whole Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But suing my own brother and sister in Court would further besmirch our parents' names.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: At the end of the day, we are brothers and sister, and we are all our parents' children.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It would also drag out the process for years and cause more distraction and distress to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, fighting this out in Court cannot be my preferred choice.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Every family will understand that family disputes do happen, but they are not something to flaunt in public.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is why I have done my best to deal with this out of the public eye.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For example, I kept my submissions to the Ministerial Committee private.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My purpose was not to pursue a fight with my siblings, but to assist the Committee in its work.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Unfortunately, my siblings made public allegations against me, and then I had no choice but to defend myself and release the statements and facts about the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I stand by the statements I have published, but I really do not want to go further if I can help it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Today, I am making this Statement in Parliament to account to Members and to Singaporeans, and to deal with this issue expeditiously so that Singaporeans can understand what it is all about and we can put the matter to rest, I hope, once and for all.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo will be making a Ministerial Statement after me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He will explain his and the Government's actions and decisions on this matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I invite Members to raise all questions, suspicions or doubts directly in this Chamber with me and my team.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have seen the questions filed by the Workers' Party (WP) MPs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is striking that the questions are general and concern broad principles and rules.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They contain no specific allegations or facts about any wrongdoing or impropriety.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But if I am mistaken and the WP has come across such allegations or facts, please raise them today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Strictly speaking, there is no Whip to lift because there is no vote to be taken.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I said this to emphasise what I expect from this debate − a robust questioning and a full airing and accounting of the public issues and allegations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is the way to dispel all the doubts, innuendo and tittle tattle that have been planted and circulated.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is the way to strengthen confidence in our institutions and our system of Government and refocus our energies on the challenges we face as a nation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The legacy of Mr Lee is much more than an old house.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Lee's legacy is Singapore and the values that we uphold.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We have built something special in Singapore − a cohesive, multiracial, meritocratic society; a fair and just society, where the same rules apply to everybody, whether you are a Minister or an ordinary citizen; whether you are the Prime Minister or the children of the founding Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My colleagues and I are in politics and in Government to fight to uphold this legacy to keep Singapore successful.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When private interests and public duties clash, we make sure that our private interests do not sway our public decisions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When allegations of impropriety and corruption are made, we take them seriously and investigate them fully.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In Singapore, everyone is equal before the law.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That the Government he built is able to withstand intense and sustained attacks on its reputation and integrity, and emerge not just untainted but, in fact, strengthened.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: This is the "house" that Mr Lee built, not 38 Oxley Road.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When Mr Lee was asked what were the most important things to him in life, he said, "My family and my country".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It pains me that this episode has put both under a cloud and done damage to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I hope, one day, I will be able to resolve the unhappiness within the family.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But, today, I stand here before Members to answer your questions, clear any doubts and show you that you have every reason to maintain your trust in me and my Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My colleagues and I will continue to serve you and work with you, as we have always done, to the best of our ability.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo will be making a related Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: So, Members who have any clarifications to make, please do so in your speeches after the Deputy Prime Minister's Ministerial Statement.
